title: 2. Did Turin and Genoa stall because of their industries?
section: T5 · Shift-share: bad luck or bad performance?
text:
T5 · Shift-share: bad luck or bad performance?
Shift-share splits the change in a city’s jobs over a period into three parts:
\[\Delta E_{city} = \text{National effect} + \text{Industry-mix effect} + \text{Local effect}\]

National effect: the jobs the city would have gained if every one of its industries had grown at the Italian average.
Industry-mix effect (hypothesis B): the extra gain or loss from having industries that did well or badly nationally.
Local effect (where Milan’s pull, hypothesis A, would show up): how the city did within the same industries compared with Italy.


viewof city = Inputs.select(cities, {label: "City", value: "Turin"})







components = ["National effect", "Industry-mix effect (B)", "Local effect (A)", "Actual change"]
ssData = ss.filter(d => d.city === city).flatMap(d => [
  {period: d.period, component: "National effect", value: d.national_pct},
  {period: d.period, component: "Industry-mix effect (B)", value: d.industry_mix_pct},
  {period: d.period, component: "Local effect (A)", value: d.local_pct},
  {period: d.period, component: "Actual change", value: d.actual_change_pct}
])
















Plot.plot({
  width,  // the page width, so text stays readable on phones
  height: 320, marginLeft: 150, marginRight: 100,
  x: {label: "% of the city's jobs at the start of the period →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: components},
  fy: {label: null, domain: ["2008-2014", "2014-2023"], axis: "right", tickFormat: d => d.replace("-", "–")},
  color: {domain: components, range: ["#86b6ef", "#eb6834", "#2a78d6", "#52514e"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(ssData, {x: "value", y: "component", fy: "period", fill: "component",
      tip: {format: {x: "+.1f", fill: false}}}),
    Plot.text(ssData, {x: d => Math.max(d.value, 0), y: "component", fy: "period", text: d => pct(d.value),
      textAnchor: "start", dx: 5, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})







html`<div class="chart-note">Without finance, ${city}'s local effect is ${ss.filter(d => d.city === city).map(d => `${pct(d.local_without_finance_pct)}% in ${d.period.replace("-", "–")}`).join(" and ")}. Reference: Italy. 11 sectors, with manufacturing separate from the rest of industry. Source: Eurostat.</div>`












TipWhat this shows · T5



Turin’s weakness has a specific timing. Between 2008 and 2014, Turin matched Italy’s performance, with services offsetting manufacturing losses: its industry-mix effect is about 0 and its local effect +0.6%. After 2014 its local effect turns negative (−1.9%, or −3.5% without finance), while the industry-mix effect stays about 0. → This fits the timing of C (no underperformance in the crisis, then decline after 2014), but not B in its broad form: Turin’s industry mix was not the problem overall.



T5 · Which sectors drive it?

viewof period = Inputs.radio(["2008-2014", "2014-2023"], {label: "Period", value: "2014-2023"})







sectorData = bySector.filter(d => d.city === city && d.period === period).flatMap(d => [

])







Plot.plot({
  width,  // the page width, so text stays readable on phones
  height: 420, marginLeft: 200,
  x: {label: "thousand jobs →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: d3.sort(bySector.filter(d => d.city === city && d.period === period),
        d => d.local_thousand_jobs).map(d => d.sector)},
  fx: {label: null, domain: ["Industry-mix effect (B)", "Local effect (A)"]},
  color: {type: "diverging", domain: [-1, 1], range: ["#e34948", "#2a78d6"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(sectorData, {x: "value", y: "sector", fx: "effect", fill: d => Math.sign(d.value),
      tip: {format: {x: "+.1f", fill: false}}}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})







Blue: more jobs than Italian trends imply; red: fewer. Sectors are sorted by their local effect. Turin’s finance jobs (+14,900 local effect in 2014–23) almost double after 2017 for reasons we could not establish.







TipWhat this shows · T5, by sector



After 2014 Turin fell behind within sectors: manufacturing employment ran 14,300 jobs below national trends and ICT ran 11,200 below. The manufacturing gap is most likely the car industry, although the sector data cannot isolate it. Genoa’s decline is of a different kind (choose Genoa above): its −5.2% local effect after 2014 is concentrated in trade, transport and hotels (−15,600 jobs), a group that includes the port and logistics, and Genoa also lost 8% of its population share and 10% of its GDP share. → For Turin, a narrow version of B (its particular industry), plus a loss of ICT jobs; for Genoa, a separate, logistics-related decline.

section: T6 · Did manufacturing-specialised provinces grow less?
text:
T6 · Did manufacturing-specialised provinces grow less?
Each dot is a northern province: how specialised in manufacturing it was in 2008 (horizontal) and how much its jobs grew by 2023 (vertical). If hypothesis B were right in its broad form, the dots would slope downwards.

viewof highlight = Inputs.checkbox(cities, {label: "Label", value: ["Milan", "Turin", "Genoa", "Bologna", "Verona", "Padua"]})







Plot.plot({
  width,  // the page width, so text stays readable on phones
  height: 440, grid: true,
  x: {label: "manufacturing specialisation in 2008 (location quotient; 1 = Italian average) →"},
  y: {label: "↑ job growth 2008–2023, %"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0]),
    Plot.ruleX([1], {strokeOpacity: 0.3}),
    Plot.linearRegressionY(provinces, {x: "manufacturing_lq_2008", y: "jobs_growth", ci: 0,
      stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "5 4"}),
    Plot.dot(provinces, {x: "manufacturing_lq_2008", y: "jobs_growth", r: 5,
      fill: d => highlight.includes(d.province) ? colourOf[d.province] : "#86b6ef",
      stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 1,
      channels: {Province: "province"},
      tip: {format: {Province: true, x: ".2f", y: "+.1f", fill: false}}}),
    // labels on the right, except Bologna (it has a close neighbour on its right)
    Plot.text(provinces.filter(d => highlight.includes(d.province) && d.province !== "Bologna"),
      {x: "manufacturing_lq_2008", y: "jobs_growth", text: "province", dx: 8, textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.text(provinces.filter(d => highlight.includes(d.province) && d.province === "Bologna"),
      {x: "manufacturing_lq_2008", y: "jobs_growth", text: "province", dx: -8, textAnchor: "end", fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})







Each dot is one of the 47 northern provinces; hover for its name. Dashed line: straight-line fit (correlation −0.09). “Manufacturing” is one broad sector in the data, so this cannot separate cars from machinery or food. Source: Eurostat.







TipWhat this shows · T6



Manufacturing in general does not explain slow growth. Manufacturing specialisation in 2008 is uncorrelated with job growth from 2008 to 2023 across the 47 northern provinces (r = −0.09). Verona (1.29) and Padua (1.40) are more specialised in manufacturing than Turin (1.21), and Bologna about as specialised (1.19), yet they grew about 11–15% while Turin grew 3%. Turin sits on the fitted line: its growth is what its specialisation predicts. → Against B in its broad form.








TipWhat this shows · what this means for hypothesis B



Hypothesis B holds only in a narrow form. Turin’s problem lies in its particular industry, not in manufacturing as such. Turin’s industry has historically been organised around one dominant car producer, while Bologna and the Veneto are known for networks of SMEs. This difference, which this project did not measure, may explain why similar levels of manufacturing specialisation produced different outcomes.

title: The answer
text:
Northern Italy is not collapsing into a single core around Milan. Milan is the North’s strongest labour market, and its lead in jobs has grown. But graduates and knowledge jobs, the mobile factors that the core–periphery model says should concentrate in the core, are no more concentrated in Milan today than they were in 2008 (knowledge jobs) or 2001 (graduates), and several other cities have grown alongside it. Turin’s and Genoa’s weaker performance is better explained by problems specific to each city than by Milan’s pull.

title: The answer
text:
Which hypothesis fits?









Hypothesis
Verdict




A
Milan’s pull
Fails in its strong form: Milan grows, but it does not absorb the North


B
Industry decline
Holds only narrowly: Turin’s particular industry, not manufacturing as such


C
Shock, then amplification
Timing fits, mechanism doesn’t: Turin declines after 2014, but shows no graduate outflow



Hypothesis A fails in its strong form: Milan grows, but it does not absorb the North. Hypothesis B holds only in a narrow form. Turin’s problem lies in its particular industry, not in manufacturing as such. Hypothesis C fits Turin’s timing (no underperformance during the crisis, then decline after 2014 that spreads into ICT). Its mechanism is not visible in the data, however: Turin shows no graduate outflow, and knowledge jobs are not shifting to Milan. The best overall account combines a narrow version of B for Turin with a separate, logistics-related decline for Genoa, while Milan grows alongside other cities rather than at their expense.

title: The answer
section: What the theory gets right and wrong
text:
What the theory gets right and wrong
The two-region core–periphery model assumes a single core, but the North is polycentric: Milan, Bologna and the Veneto all grow, so agglomeration gains are spread across several centres. The model’s dispersion forces are visible, in the form of housing costs (Helpman, 1998) spreading Milan’s population into its belt. Martin’s (1999) critique also applies, because the model ignores firm structure and institutions. Turin’s industry has historically been organised around one dominant car producer, while Bologna and the Veneto are known for networks of SMEs. This difference, which this project did not measure, may explain why similar levels of manufacturing specialisation produced different outcomes.

title: Method & data
text:
The project uses Krugman’s (1991) core–periphery model (Lectures 7–8) in the “footloose entrepreneur” version of Forslid and Ottaviano (2003):

Graduates and knowledge workers are mobile. They move to wherever their career prospects are better. Each firm needs skilled people, so firms move with them.
Manufacturing workers with skills specific to one local industry, and the less mobile population, stay put. Their spending keeps demand in the periphery.
Mechanism: when trading between regions gets cheaper, a small advantage grows through circular cumulative causation (more graduates → more firms → more varied jobs → more graduates). Past the break point, skilled workers and their firms concentrate in one region.
Extensions used: housing costs in the core as a force pushing activity out (Helpman, 1998); Martin’s (1999) critique that the model ignores institutions and firm structure.

title: Method & data
text:
Limitations

The car industry is hidden inside “manufacturing”, so hypothesis B is inferred for Turin rather than measured.
Jobs data starts only in 2008.
Jobs are counted at the workplace and graduates at residence, so commuting into Milan blurs the comparison.
Turin’s finance jobs almost double between 2017 and 2023 for reasons we could not establish (possibly a change in where a large bank registers its staff). Results that depend on finance are reported with and without it.
Graduate migration data covers only 2019–2023, so Turin’s net gain of graduates is a recent snapshot.
The methods are descriptive: they show patterns consistent with or against each hypothesis, not proof of cause.

Next step. The natural extension is to test the car industry directly, using ISTAT data on detailed sectors, so that hypothesis B for Turin is measured rather than inferred.

title: Is Milan absorbing the North?
text:
Is northern Italy collapsing into a single core around Milan, as the core–periphery model predicts, or did the old industrial cities (Turin, Genoa) stall because of what they specialised in? Or did the decline of their industries trigger the move towards Milan?

Milan, Turin and Genoa were once the “industrial triangle” that industrialised Italy. Today Milan seems to keep growing, while Turin and Genoa seem to stand still. This project asks why, and whether a model from the course can explain it.

title: Is Milan absorbing the North?
section: Where the question comes from: my observations
text:
Where the question comes from: my observations
I live in Turin, and the question started from what I see around me. These observations are where the ideas come from; they are not evidence. Each one was turned into something the data could check.

An idea to test: “Turin trains, Milan employs”. Turin is a big university city (Politecnico, University of Turin), so it may produce many graduates but not keep them, while Milan employs them.

title: Is Milan absorbing the North?
text:
The theory: the core–periphery model
I use Krugman’s (1991) core–periphery model from Lectures 7–8, in the “footloose entrepreneur” version of Forslid and Ottaviano (2003):

Who moves: graduates and knowledge workers. They go where career prospects are better, and firms follow them.
Who stays: manufacturing workers whose skills fit one local industry (for example cars in Turin), and the less mobile population.
The mechanism: as trade and communication get cheaper, a small advantage grows. More graduates attract more firms, which create more varied jobs, which attract more graduates. In the end, one region becomes the core.

The model says one city will win, but not which one. History and shocks decide that.

title: Is Milan absorbing the North?
text:
Three possible answers (hypotheses)










Hypothesis
The story in one sentence
What it predicts




A
Milan’s pull: the mechanism inside the core–periphery model
Graduates move to Milan, firms follow them, so Milan becomes even more attractive while Turin is left behind
Graduates and knowledge jobs concentrate in Milan faster than people; other cities lose share


B
Industry decline: a shock from outside the model
Cars, steel and shipbuilding shrank for global reasons; Turin and Genoa would have stalled even without Milan
Turin’s and Genoa’s losses come from the industries they had; manufacturing-specialised cities grow less


C
Both, in sequence
The industry decline weakened Turin first, then Milan’s pull made it worse
Industry losses first; then the local decline and the graduate outflow speed up



The predictions were written down before looking at the data, so that the data could prove them wrong.

What the model predicts. In the footloose-entrepreneur version of the core–periphery model, graduates are the mobile factor and firms follow them. If the North is tipping into a single core, Milan’s share of graduates and knowledge jobs should rise faster than its share of people, and the other cities should lose ground.

text:
T2 · Are graduates concentrating in Milan?
The censuses of 2001, 2011 and 2021 count graduates by province. The ratio below is each city’s share of northern graduates divided by its share of northern population.

censusCities = ["Milan area", "Turin", "Genoa", "Bologna", "Verona", "Padua", "Bergamo", "Brescia"]







viewof shownC = Inputs.checkbox(censusCities, {label: "Cities", value: ["Milan area", "Turin", "Genoa", "Bologna"]})







Plot.plot({
  width,  // the page width, so text stays readable on phones
  height: 340, marginRight: 110,
  x: {label: null, tickFormat: "d", ticks: [2001, 2011, 2021]},
  y: {label: "share of graduates ÷ share of population", grid: true, zero: true},
  color: {...colourFor(shownC), legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], {strokeOpacity: 0.5, strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.lineY(census.filter(d => shownC.includes(d.city)), {x: "year", y: "graduate_concentration",
      stroke: "city", strokeWidth: 2, marker: "circle",
      tip: {format: {x: "d", y: ".2f", stroke: true}}}),
    Plot.text(census.filter(d => shownC.includes(d.city)), Plot.selectLast({x: "year", y: "graduate_concentration",
      z: "city", text: "city", textAnchor: "start", dx: 8, fill: "currentColor"}))
  ]
})







Milan area = Milan + Monza (Monza was part of Milan in 2001). Graduate definitions differ slightly between censuses, so only shares are compared. As more people everywhere get degrees, these ratios naturally drift towards 1. Sources: Eurostat (2001), ISTAT (2011, 2021).







TipWhat this shows · T2



Milan’s graduate concentration ratio did not rise (1.36 in 2001, 1.32 in 2021). Graduates, the mobile factor in the model, are no more concentrated in Milan than twenty years ago, while Genoa’s ratio falls the most (1.33 → 1.15). → Against A.

T8 · Turin trains, Milan employs?

trainsLong = trains.flatMap(d => [
  {city: d.city, what: "Graduates produced by local universities", value: d.share_of_graduates_produced_pct},
  {city: d.city, what: "Graduates aged 25–49 living there", value: d.share_of_resident_graduates_25_49_pct}
])







Plot.plot({
  width,  // the page width, so text stays readable on phones
  height: 360,
  x: {axis: null, domain: ["Graduates produced by local universities", "Graduates aged 25–49 living there"]},
  fx: {label: null, domain: trains.map(d => d.city)},
  y: {label: "% of northern Italy", grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["Graduates produced by local universities", "Graduates aged 25–49 living there"],
          range: ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(trainsLong, {x: "what", y: "value", fx: "city", fill: "what",
      tip: {format: {y: ".1f", x: false, fx: true, fill: true}}}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})







Produced: average 2019–2023, northern universities, online universities excluded (Ministry of University). Resident: census 2021 (ISTAT). Residence is not place of work.







TipWhat this shows · T8



Every big university city produces more graduates than it keeps as residents: Turin keeps 0.60 of its “fair share”, Milan 0.66, Bologna 0.43 and Padua 0.45. So Turin does not stand out from Milan here. → The “Turin trains, Milan employs” idea is not supported as something specific to Turin.

title: 1. Is the North becoming a single core?
section: T9 · Around Milan: a place to live, not to work
text:
T9 · Around Milan: a place to live, not to work
Select Monza-Brianza, Bergamo and Brescia in the first chart above, with the measure set to Population and then to Knowledge jobs.






TipWhat this shows · T9



Where Milan does reshape its surroundings, it does so as a place to live rather than to work. Monza, Bergamo and Brescia gained population share but lost 6–8% of their knowledge-job share. This is consistent with Milan’s housing costs pushing residents outwards while the jobs stay in the city, although housing costs were not measured here. → Partly A: Milan’s core spreads as a place to live, not to work.
